title: Transactions
lead: Transaction semantics, ACID, serial schedules, conflicts and serializability.
goals: ACID and the source interleaving example

sections.title: Transaction model and concurrent execution
sections.html:
A transaction groups database operations into one unit beginning with BEGIN and ending in COMMIT or ABORT/ROLLBACK. A commit accepts its changes; an abort removes its effects. The abstract model represents access to named objects using Rᵢ(A) and Wᵢ(A).

The source transfers £100 between checking and savings by debiting one account and crediting the other. The intermediate state is not the completed transaction result. External effects outside the database are not automatically rolled back by the DBMS.

Concurrent execution overlaps work to improve resource utilisation, throughput and response time. Correctness requires controlling the resulting interleaving of read and write operations.

PDF pp. 1–11

sections.title: ACID and the source interleaving example
sections.html:
Atomicity means all-or-nothing effects. Consistency requires transactions and enforced constraints to preserve valid database states. Isolation constrains interference between concurrent transactions. Durability preserves committed effects through the failures covered by the recovery model.

Logging and shadow paging support atomicity and durability; pessimistic or optimistic concurrency control supports isolation. Application logic remains responsible for expressing a correct transaction.

The source starts A = B = 1000, transfers 100 in T1 and applies 6% interest in T2. The two serial orders give (954,1166) or (960,1160), both totalling 2120. An invalid interleaving gives (954,1160), totalling 2114. Preserving each transaction’s internal order alone is insufficient.

PDF pp. 12–23

sections.title: Schedules and conflicting operations
sections.html:
A schedule contains operations from several transactions while preserving each transaction’s own operation order. A serial schedule runs transactions without interleaving. A serializable schedule has an effect equivalent to an appropriate serial execution under the chosen equivalence notion.

Two operations conflict when they belong to different transactions, access the same object and at least one writes. Read–read pairs do not conflict. Read–write, write–read and write–write orders can affect values observed or retained.

The source relates these conflicts to unrepeatable reads, dirty reads and overwriting uncommitted data. Commit/abort ordering also matters for recovery; serializability alone does not specify every failure-handling property.

PDF pp. 24–31

sections.title: Conflict serializability and precedence graphs
sections.html:
Two schedules are conflict equivalent if they contain the same transaction operations and preserve the order of every conflicting pair. A schedule is conflict serializable when it is conflict equivalent to a serial schedule.

Construct a graph with one vertex per transaction. Add Tᵢ → Tⱼ whenever an operation of Tᵢ precedes a conflicting operation of Tⱼ on the same object. Include every such pair, not only neighbouring operations.

The schedule is conflict serializable exactly when the graph is acyclic. A topological order gives an equivalent serial order. A cycle rejects conflict serializability even if one particular numerical execution happens to produce an acceptable result.

PDF pp. 32–42

sections.title: View serializability and durability
sections.html:
View equivalence preserves which reads obtain initial values, which transaction each other read obtains its value from, and which transaction performs the final write of each object. A schedule is view serializable if it is view equivalent to a serial schedule.

Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable, but blind writes allow additional view-serializable schedules. Testing the broader property is harder; the course uses conflict serializability as the practical basis for locking protocols.

Durability is a separate requirement: acknowledged commits must survive a crash. Logging or shadow paging supplies the persistent information needed to preserve committed changes and remove aborted work.

PDF pp. 43–48

quiz.question: Is R1(A), W2(A), W1(B), R2(B) conflict-serializable?
options: Yes, in the order T1 then T2
Yes, in the order T2 then T1
No, because the graph has a cycle
There is insufficient information because two objects are involved
quiz.explanation: Both R1(A) before W2(A) and W1(B) before R2(B) create T1 → T2. There is no edge in the reverse direction.

source.summary: Lecture 19 introduces transactions, ACID, execution schedules, conflicts, and two serializability criteria. A dependency graph checks conflict serializability, while logging or shadow paging supports atomicity and durability.
